title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
description: Bunyan's spiritual autobiography, written in Bedford Gaol during his twelve-year imprisonment for preaching without a licence, which records his agonising struggle with doubt, temptation, and the assurance of salvation.
plot_or_argument: Bunyan traces his life from a childhood of swearing and bell-ringing through his conversion under John Gifford, his long torments of doubt and despair, his reading of Luther's Commentary on Galatians, and his final assurance of grace; the narrative is organised around biblical typology rather than chronology.
narrative_structure: A first-person retrospective narrative in numbered paragraphs, with scriptural glosses on the margins, following the pattern of the Pauline conversion.
principal_characters: John Bunyan (the narrator); John Gifford; his first wife; his second wife Elizabeth; the Bedford congregation
meter_and_prosody: Vigorous, colloquial prose saturated with biblical language, especially the Psalms, Paul, and Hebrews.
historical_context: Written in 1666 during Bunyan's first long imprisonment (1660-72) and published in the same year with a preface addressed to his Bedford congregation; a seventh edition appeared before his death.
literary_significance: The greatest spiritual autobiography in English and a foundational text of the Protestant confessional tradition; it supplied the raw material of inner experience that Bunyan transformed into the allegory of The Pilgrim's Progress.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1666. Standard edition: The Pilgrim's Progress (N. H. Keeble, ed., Oxford World's Classics, 1984), which includes Grace Abounding; also Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (Roger Sharrock, ed., Oxford University Press, 1962).

title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part I)
description: Bunyan's allegorical dream-narrative of the journey of Christian from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, begun in his second imprisonment and published in 1678; it is the most popular and most translated work of English prose fiction.
plot_or_argument: Christian, burdened with sin, is directed by Evangelist to the Wicket Gate; he passes through the Slough of Despond, the House of the Interpreter, the Cross where his burden falls, the Hill of Difficulty, the Valley of Humiliation where he fights Apollyon, the Valley of the Shadow of Death, Vanity Fair where Faithful is martyred, Doubting Castle where he is imprisoned by Giant Despair, and the Delectable Mountains, until he crosses the river into the Celestial City.
narrative_structure: A framed dream-vision in two stages of journey, with episodic encounters, embedded verses, and the author's Apology as a preface.
principal_characters: Christian; Evangelist; Pliable; Obstinate; Mr Worldly Wiseman; Faithful; Talkative; Hopeful; Apollyon; Giant Despair; Christiana (Part II); Interpreter; Great-heart
literary_form: allegory; dream vision; prose fiction; spiritual narrative
meter_and_prosody: Plain, colloquial prose interwoven with biblical phrase and with short verses at intervals.
historical_context: Composed during Bunyan's second imprisonment (1675-6) and published in February 1678 by Nathaniel Ponder, whose shop sign gave the book the nickname 'The Pilgrim's Progress from Ponder's'; it went through ten editions in Bunyan's lifetime.
literary_significance: The supreme English prose allegory and, with Robinson Crusoe, one of the two founding works of the English novel; it has never been out of print, has been translated into more than two hundred languages, and has shaped the imaginative vocabulary of the English-speaking world ('Vanity Fair', 'the Slough of Despond', 'Doubting Castle').
bibliographical_notes: First published 1678 (Nathaniel Ponder); third edition with additions 1679. Standard edition: The Pilgrim's Progress (N. H. Keeble, ed., Oxford World's Classics, 1984); also The Pilgrim's Progress (Roger Sharrock, ed., Oxford University Press, 1960).

title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part II)
description: The second part of Bunyan's allegory, in which Christian's wife Christiana, with her four sons and the neighbour Mercy, undertakes the same pilgrimage under the protection of the valiant Great-heart.
plot_or_argument: Christiana repents her earlier harshness to Christian and sets out with Mercy and the children; guided by Great-heart, they pass through the same places Christian knew, overcome Giant Grim and the other giants, and reach the Celestial City.
narrative_structure: A framed dream-vision following Part I's itinerary with a female party and a protective escort.
principal_characters: Christiana; Mercy; Matthew; Samuel; Joseph; James; Great-heart; Mr Prudence; Mr Piety; Giant Grim; Despondency's daughter Much-afraid
meter_and_prosody: Plain prose with interpolated verses, gentler and more social in tone than Part I.
historical_context: Published in 1684, six years after Part I, in response to its enormous popularity and to the many spurious continuations that had appeared.
literary_significance: Completes the allegory with a domestic and communal pilgrimage that has been widely read as a feminist counterpart to Part I; it is normally printed with Part I in every edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1684. Standard edition: The Pilgrim's Progress (N. H. Keeble, ed., Oxford World's Classics, 1984), which includes both parts.

title: The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
description: Bunyan's realistic prose narrative, presented as a dialogue between Mr. Wiseman and Mr. Attentive, of the life and unrepentant death of the wicked tradesman Badman; it is often regarded as the first English novel in prose.
plot_or_argument: Wiseman recounts Badman's apprenticeship, his fraudulent bankruptcy, his mercenary marriage, his debauchery, his illnesses, and his death without repentance, drawing moral and economic lessons from each episode.
narrative_structure: A dialogue-narrative in which one speaker relates a life-story and the other comments; the episodic structure anticipates the picaresque novel.
principal_characters: Mr Badman; Mr Wiseman; Mr Attentive; Badman's first wife; his second wife; his apprentices
meter_and_prosody: Vivid, colloquial prose of trade, tavern, and household, unusually detailed in its social observation.
historical_context: Published in 1658, in the last months of the Protectorate, as a warning against the sins of trade and the false peace of the unregenerate.
literary_significance: A pioneering work of English prose realism and a major source for the social and economic history of the Interregnum; its detailed depiction of commercial fraud and domestic misery has no earlier English equivalent.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1658. Standard edition: The Life and Death of Mr Badman (James F. Forrest and Richard L. Greaves, eds., Oxford University Press, 1984); The Works of John Bunyan (George Offor, ed., 1860-2).

title: The Holy War Made by Shaddai upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World
description: Bunyan's second great allegory, a military and spiritual epic of the town of Mansoul, built by Shaddai, captured by Diabolus, and recovered by his son Emmanuel; it is a complex allegory of the soul's fall and redemption.
plot_or_argument: Shaddai builds Mansoul and gives it law; Diabolus besieges and takes it; Emmanuel, Shaddai's son, wages war to recover it, captures and pardons the town, and appoints officers; Diabolus returns by stealth and the town must be continually defended.
narrative_structure: A prose epic in four parts with an allegorical cast of named officers, captains, and townspeople.
principal_characters: Shaddai; Emmanuel; Diabolus; the Lord Secretary; Captain Credence; Mr Conscience; Mr Recorder; the captains Boanerges; the towns of Mansoul
meter_and_prosody: Plain prose with an elaborate allegorical nomenclature and occasional verses.
historical_context: Published in 1682 with a copperplate frontispiece, four years after Part I of The Pilgrim's Progress, and dedicated to the reader in an allegorical address.
literary_significance: Bunyan's most ambitious and most learned allegory, and a major work of Puritan theology in narrative form; it has been judged more complex but less popular than The Pilgrim's Progress.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1682. Standard edition: The Holy War (Roger Sharrock and James Forrest, eds., Oxford University Press, 1980); The Works of John Bunyan (George Offor, ed., 1860-2).
